Doctor: Thanks for coming in. I'm seeing a 38-year-old female today for dizziness. Tell me what has been happening.
Patient: It started about a week ago. When I roll over in bed or tip my head back to reach a high shelf, the room spins for maybe thirty seconds and then it settles down.
Doctor: Does the spinning ever happen when you are sitting still or walking around?
Patient: No, only when I change my head position. I feel a little queasy afterward, but I haven't thrown up.
Doctor: Any hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or fullness in the ear?
Patient: No, my hearing seems the same as always, and no ringing.
Doctor: Any headache, double vision, trouble speaking, or weakness in your arms or legs?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any recent cold, ear infection, or head injury?
Patient: No. I take levothyroxine 75 mcg once a day for an underactive thyroid, and that's my only medicine.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure is 118 over 74 and your pulse is 72. Your eye movements and facial strength are normal, and your hearing is normal to finger rub. On the Dix-Hallpike maneuver with your head turned to the right, you had a burst of upward-beating nystagmus with the spinning feeling that lasted about twenty seconds, and the left side was normal. This is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo from the right posterior canal. I'd like to do an Epley maneuver now.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good.
Doctor: All done. How do you feel?
Patient: Much better, just a little off-balance.
Doctor: That's expected. Sleep with your head propped up on two pillows for the next two nights. I don't need to start any medication. Come back in two weeks if the spinning continues, and go to the emergency room right away if you get a severe headache, double vision, or weakness.
summary: A 38-year-old female presented with one week of brief episodes of spinning vertigo triggered by rolling over in bed or tipping her head back, with mild queasiness but no vomiting, hearing loss, headache, double vision or weakness. She takes levothyroxine 75 mcg once a day for an underactive thyroid. Blood pressure was 118 over 74 and pulse 72, and a right Dix-Hallpike maneuver produced upward-beating nystagmus with vertigo. The clinician diagnosed benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the right posterior canal and performed an Epley maneuver, after which she felt much better. She was advised to sleep with her head propped up for two nights, with no medication started, follow-up in two weeks if symptoms persist, and emergency return precautions.

This is a hospital ward progress dictation on a 32-year-old male with Crohn's disease, hospital day 3. He was admitted two days ago with a Crohn's disease flare. He is a recent readmission, because he was discharged from this hospital about three weeks ago after a flare that was treated with intravenous steroids. He has ileocolonic Crohn's disease diagnosed years ago and takes adalimumab 40 mg every other week. He has a documented sulfa allergy, which caused a diffuse rash, so sulfasalazine is not an option for him.

At home he was finishing a prednisone taper from the last admission. He first told me he was taking prednisone 10 mg daily when the symptoms came back, correction, he brought the bottle in and he was actually taking 20 mg daily and had not tapered below that. He was also using loperamide as needed for the diarrhea and ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily.

Interval history, he reports eight to ten loose watery stools a day including nighttime stools, with crampy right lower quadrant abdominal pain and about six pounds of weight loss over the last month. Overnight he had five stools and some nausea. He denies fever, vomiting, blood in the stool, perianal pain and mouth sores.

Current inpatient medications are methylprednisolone 30 mg IV every 12 hours, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for VTE prophylaxis, ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours as needed for nausea, and lactated Ringer's at 100 mL per hour. Potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth was given yesterday for repletion.

Vitals this morning, temperature 99.1, heart rate 96, blood pressure 112 over 68, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air.

On exam he is thin but in no distress. Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant, no rebound, no guarding, and no distension. Bowel sounds are present. Perianal exam shows no fistula or abscess, and there are no oral ulcers.

Data, hemoglobin 10.1, WBC 11.8, platelets 480, CRP 78, albumin 3.0, potassium 3.4 on admission and 3.9 this morning, creatinine 0.8. Ferritin is low at 14. C. difficile PCR and stool culture were both negative. CT enterography on admission showed a 15 cm segment of terminal ileal wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and no abscess or obstruction.

My impression is a moderate to severe Crohn's disease flare in a patient on adalimumab, with anemia, hypokalemia that has now been corrected, and low albumin.

As for management, one, the home prednisone is discontinued and he will stay on methylprednisolone 30 mg IV every 12 hours for now. Two, stop loperamide and avoid antimotility agents during the flare. Three, send an adalimumab trough level with antibodies, and given the flare on every other week dosing I will intensify adalimumab to 40 mg weekly starting with the next scheduled dose. If there is no clear improvement by hospital day 5 we will discuss infliximab with the attending. Four, continue enoxaparin and ondansetron as needed. Five, stop oral ferrous sulfate because it worsens his stomach upset, and give iron sucrose 200 mg IV for the iron deficiency. Six, dietitian consult for nutrition support. Seven, repeat CRP and BMP in the morning. He will not receive sulfasalazine because of the sulfa allergy. Expected discharge is in three to four days on a prednisone taper, with GI clinic follow-up within one week, and he understands to return for worsening pain, fever or bleeding.

Hospital day 3 for a 68-year-old female admitted with symptomatic hyponatremia. She presented two days before admission with confusion, nausea, headache, and unsteady walking. She works rotating night shifts at a distribution warehouse with an irregular sleep and meal schedule, and she reports drinking large amounts of water and tea to stay awake on shifts and often skipping meals when her shift changes. Her primary care physician started hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily three weeks ago for HTN, and she also takes sertraline 50 mg daily for depression. She denies vomiting, diarrhea, seizure, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

No acute events overnight. Her serum sodium was 118 on arrival, 123 after two 100 mL boluses of 3% saline in the emergency department, and 126 this morning, so the correction has stayed well under the eight-point daily limit. Her mentation has cleared, and the headache and nausea have resolved.

Vitals today: BP 138/82, HR 76, RR 16, temp 98.1 F, SpO2 97% on room air. Weight is 71 kg, unchanged from admission. She is alert and oriented, mucous membranes are moist, there is no peripheral edema, jugular venous pressure is normal, and the lungs are clear. She appears euvolemic.

Labs this morning show serum osmolality 258, urine osmolality 412, TSH 2.1, morning cortisol normal, potassium 3.3, creatinine 0.7, glucose 96, and an inappropriately elevated urine sodium.

My impression is symptomatic hypotonic hyponatremia, most likely thiazide-induced, with possible contribution from sertraline and high free water intake. She also has mild hypokalemia, and her HTN needs a new regimen.

Hydrochlorothiazide is discontinued permanently and will be listed as an adverse reaction. Continue sertraline 50 mg daily with close monitoring for now. Fluid restriction to 1.2 liters per day. Start amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure. Give potassium chloride 20 mEq by mouth twice today. Repeat BMP every 8 hours today, then daily. Because of her night-shift schedule, we will tie her medications to a consistent anchor time relative to when she wakes rather than clock time, supply a weekly pillbox, and ask pharmacy for a written schedule. She will get a printed fluid target for work shifts, and a repeat sodium check is planned three days after discharge at a lab draw time that fits her days off. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if sodium continues to rise and she stays asymptomatic.

Her serum sodium rose from 118 on arrival to 126 after 3% saline and is now stable, with cleared mentation and an euvolemic exam. Urine osmolality was 412 with an inappropriately elevated urine sodium, and potassium was 3.3. The impression is thiazide-induced hyponatremia with mild hypokalemia and HTN. Hydrochlorothiazide is stopped, amlodipine 5 mg daily and potassium chloride are started, fluids are restricted, and a shift-adapted medication schedule and lab recheck are planned before discharge.

Telehealth video visit. The patient joined from home on a tablet with good audio and video, and she was alone for the visit. This is a follow-up for progressive dysphagia in a 24-year-old female, to review her recent endoscopy results.

History: She reports about eight months of trouble swallowing solid foods that has gotten steadily worse over the past two months. At first only bread and dry meat would stick in the mid-chest, but now rice and raw vegetables stick as well, and she has to drink water after every bite and eat very slowly. Two weeks ago a piece of chicken lodged in her chest for about twenty minutes before she brought it back up with regurgitation. She also describes mild chest discomfort with swallowing and has lost about 6 pounds. She denies trouble swallowing liquids, vomiting blood, black stools, and fever.

Past history includes asthma, allergic rhinitis, and eczema since childhood. EGD six weeks ago showed concentric rings, linear furrows, and white exudates in the esophagus, and biopsies showed 58 eosinophils per high-power field, consistent with eosinophilic esophagitis.

Medications and adherence: After the EGD she was prescribed omeprazole 20 mg daily and fluticasone HFA 110 mcg, 2 puffs swallowed twice daily. She also uses cetirizine for allergies, albuterol inhaler as needed for asthma, and ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for back pain. She has not been taking the fluticasone consistently, only about two or three days a week, because the copay was too high and she is stretching the inhaler. She has also skipped omeprazole on days when money was short. She first said she takes cetirizine 20 mg daily, but when she held the bottle up to the camera it read 10 mg, and she confirmed she takes one 10 mg tablet daily.

Social: She has no car and needs two buses, about ninety minutes each way, to reach the hospital, and she missed the GI nurse visit last month for that reason.

Home measurements: BP 108/66, HR 74, temperature 98.4 F, weight 128 pounds, down from 134 pounds at the last clinic visit. Video exam: she looks comfortable and thin, speaks in full sentences without audible wheeze or respiratory distress, has no facial or lip swelling, and no visible jaundice. Labs from her primary care office last week: hemoglobin 13.1 and an elevated absolute eosinophil count of 620.

Impression: Progressive dysphagia due to eosinophilic esophagitis, with a recent food impaction and weight loss, undertreated because of medication cost and limited transportation. Asthma and allergic rhinitis are stable; she has used albuterol rarely.

Management: Increase omeprazole from 20 mg once daily to 40 mg twice daily. Continue fluticasone HFA 110 mcg, 2 puffs swallowed twice daily, and our pharmacist and social worker will apply for a manufacturer assistance program and send a ninety-day supply to a mail-order pharmacy so she does not have to travel. Stop ibuprofen because it can irritate the esophagus and worsen asthma; use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain instead. Continue cetirizine 10 mg daily and albuterol as needed. Telehealth dietitian visit to discuss a milk and wheat elimination trial. Repeat EGD with biopsies in about ten weeks, scheduled the same day as a dietitian visit with a hospital transportation voucher so that she needs only one trip. Reviewed food impaction precautions: cut food into small pieces, chew thoroughly, and go to the emergency department if she cannot swallow saliva or has chest pain after a stuck bite. Nurse phone call in one week to check on adherence and cost, and a video follow-up in four weeks.

Chief Complaint: Shortness of breath and wheezing.

HPI: 61-year-old female with asthma, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes who presents by ambulance with two days of worsening shortness of breath, wheezing, and cough that was worse overnight. She had four days of runny nose and sore throat beforehand. She used her albuterol inhaler about every hour today, roughly eight to ten puffs, with only brief relief. She ran out of her controller inhaler about two weeks ago because the pharmacy is far from her home and she has no car and no reliable ride; her daughter works days and could not bring her in earlier. About ten days ago a clinic started propranolol 20 mg twice daily for hand tremor. She denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, hemoptysis, and vomiting. She has had no prior intubations and one hospital admission for asthma three years ago.

Home medications (reviewed with the patient and her daughter by phone): fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation twice daily (ran out two weeks ago), albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed, lisinopril 20 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg twice daily, and metformin. The patient first stated metformin 500 mg twice daily; correction, her daughter read the bottle over the phone and it is 1000 mg twice daily. No known drug allergies.

ROS: Positive for cough and rhinorrhea. Negative for fever, chest pain, orthopnea, abdominal pain, and dysuria.

Physical Exam: BP 156/92, HR 112, RR 28, temp 98.9 F, SpO2 89% on room air. Sitting upright, speaking in short phrases, using accessory muscles. Diffuse expiratory wheezes with prolonged expiratory phase and diminished air movement at both bases. Heart tachycardic and regular. No jugular venous distension, no leg edema. Peak flow 160 L/min (predicted about 380).

ED Course / Results: Received continuous albuterol-ipratropium nebulizers 2.5 mg/0.5 mg for three doses, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV once, magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes, and oxygen 2 L by nasal cannula, with SpO2 improving to 95%. After treatment: HR 98, RR 20, wheezing much improved, peak flow 280 L/min, and SpO2 96% on room air. Chest x-ray showed hyperinflation with no infiltrate, effusion, or pneumothorax. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST changes. VBG pH 7.36, pCO2 42. WBC 12.4, glucose 238 mg/dL, potassium 3.4, bicarbonate 24 with a normal anion gap, creatinine 0.9, troponin negative.

Medical Decision Making: Moderate to severe acute asthma exacerbation, likely triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection, loss of controller therapy for two weeks, and the new non-selective beta-blocker propranolol. Considered pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, and pneumothorax; the chest x-ray, ECG, normal troponin, and rapid response to bronchodilators make these unlikely. Hyperglycemia is from steroids on top of type 2 diabetes, with no evidence of DKA. Propranolol is discontinued because non-selective beta-blockers worsen bronchospasm; I will message her primary care physician about tremor management. She also needs a higher-dose controller, so fluticasone-salmeterol will be increased from 250/50 to 500/50 one inhalation twice daily.

Disposition: Observed for five hours with sustained improvement; discharge home. Prescriptions: prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days, fluticasone-salmeterol 500/50 one inhalation twice daily, and albuterol HFA as needed. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily and metformin 1000 mg twice daily with extra home glucose checks while on prednisone. Because she has no car, the pharmacy filled the prescriptions here before she left (meds-to-beds) with a 30-day supply, and a social worker arranged a ride home with her daughter after work and a transportation voucher for the primary care visit in three days; the clinic will also offer a video visit. A nurse will call tomorrow to check on her breathing. Return precautions reviewed: worsening shortness of breath, inability to speak full sentences, blue lips, or no relief from albuterol.

SpO2 was 89% on room air with a respiratory rate of 28, wheezes and a peak flow of 160 L/min, and chest x-ray showed hyperinflation without infiltrate. She improved after albuterol-ipratropium, methylprednisolone, magnesium sulfate and oxygen. The impression was an acute asthma exacerbation with hyperglycemia, and propranolol was discontinued. She was discharged on prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days and a higher-dose controller, with medications supplied before leaving, a ride arranged, and primary care follow-up in three days.

Doctor: Thanks for coming in. I'm seeing a 31-year-old male here for follow-up of a kidney stone. I understand you were in the emergency department five days ago.
Patient: Yes, they did a CT and found a stone on the right side, about five millimeters. They sent me home with tamsulosin and ibuprofen.
Doctor: How have things been since then?
Patient: The pain is still there, mostly in my right side and back, and it comes in waves. I strain my urine like they told me, but no stone has come out.
Family member: He's my son and he lives with me. Since this morning he's been throwing up, and he hasn't kept much water down for two days. I also saw pink urine in the toilet.
Doctor: Any fever, chills, or burning when you urinate?
Patient: No fever, no chills, and no burning.
Doctor: How are you taking the medicines?
Patient: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg every evening, and ibuprofen 600 mg about three times a day for the pain.
Doctor: Okay. Your temperature is 98.6, your pulse is 92, and your blood pressure is 138 over 86. You are tender over the right flank, your belly is soft, and there are no peritoneal signs. The urine dipstick shows 3 plus blood, with no nitrite and no leukocyte esterase. Your creatinine came back at 1.3, up from 0.9 in the emergency department, and the bedside ultrasound shows mild swelling of the right kidney, which is called hydronephrosis.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It tells me the stone is still blocking the right ureter, you are a bit dehydrated from the vomiting, and the ibuprofen is not helping your kidneys right now. So I'm stopping the ibuprofen and starting acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed. I'm also giving you ondansetron 4 mg dissolving tablets every 8 hours as needed for nausea. Keep taking the tamsulosin every evening and drink at least three liters of fluid a day.
Family member: Should we go to the hospital?
Doctor: Not right now, but I want you seen by urology in three days, and if the stone has not passed within a week they will talk to you about ureteroscopy. Go to the emergency room if you get a fever, have pain that is not controlled, cannot keep fluids down, or make very little urine. Once the stone passes, we will arrange a 24-hour urine collection to look for the cause.
summary: A 31-year-old male returned to urgent care five days after an emergency visit for a 5 mm right kidney stone, with persistent right flank and back pain, vomiting since this morning, pink urine and poor fluid intake, as described partly by his mother. He denies fever, chills and burning when he urinates. He has right flank tenderness, 3 plus blood on dipstick, creatinine 1.3 up from 0.9, and mild right hydronephrosis on bedside ultrasound. The impression is a stone still obstructing the right ureter with mild dehydration. Ibuprofen is stopped, acetaminophen and ondansetron are started, tamsulosin continues, and he should drink fluids and see urology in three days.

Doctor: Hello, I'm seeing an 83-year-old female who fell at home this afternoon. Can you tell me what happened?
Patient: I was walking to the kitchen and my foot caught the edge of the rug. I landed on my right side and bumped my head on the cabinet.
Doctor: Did you black out before or after you fell?
Patient: No, I remember the whole thing. I didn't pass out.
Doctor: Any neck pain, vomiting, confusion, or vision changes?
Patient: No neck pain, no vomiting, and I feel clear-headed. I just have a sore spot on my forehead.
Doctor: I see you have atrial fibrillation. Which blood thinner do you take?
Patient: Apixaban, 5 mg twice a day. I took this morning's dose.
Doctor: Any other medicines?
Patient: No, that's the only one.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure is 142 over 84 and your pulse is 78. You have a three-centimeter bruise with mild swelling over the right forehead, but the skin is intact. Your neck moves freely without tenderness, your hip and wrist exams are normal, and you walked steadily with the nurse. The CT scan of the head shows no bleeding and no fracture. So this was a mechanical fall, and you have a scalp contusion without a head bleed.
Patient: Do I stop the blood thinner?
Doctor: No, keep taking the apixaban twice a day, since the scan is clear. Use ice on the forehead and acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for soreness. Your daughter should stay with you tonight, and come back right away if you get a worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, or unusual sleepiness. I'll also have physical therapy look at your home safety, please remove loose rugs, and see your primary care doctor in a week.
Patient: Okay, thank you.

She has a three-centimeter bruise with mild swelling over the right forehead, a normal neck, hip and wrist exam, and a CT scan of the head showing no bleeding or fracture. The impression is a mechanical fall with a scalp contusion and no head bleed. She should continue apixaban twice a day, use ice and acetaminophen as needed, have her daughter stay with her tonight, remove loose rugs, and see primary care in a week with return precautions.

Seen in the infectious disease clinic for a painful blistering rash. This 82-year-old male developed burning pain over the right side of his lower chest and back five days ago, and a rash of clustered blisters appeared three days ago, wrapping around the right side of his trunk toward the front. The pain is a constant burning, rated 7 out of 10, with sharp stabbing episodes, and even his shirt touching the skin is painful, which wakes him at night. He remembers having chickenpox as a child and has never received the recombinant zoster vaccine. He denies fever, headache, eye pain, vision changes, facial rash, and new weakness. He has not been on steroids or any immunosuppressive medication.

Past history includes HTN treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and chronic kidney disease stage 3 with a baseline creatinine around 1.5. He has no known drug allergies. He lives with his wife. He tried over-the-counter acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours with little relief.

On exam today, temperature 98.2 F, heart rate 72, blood pressure 146/84, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He is comfortable at rest but winces when the rash is touched. There are grouped vesicles on erythematous bases in a band along the right T8 dermatome from the mid back around to the upper abdomen, stopping at the midline, with some early crusting and no pus, spreading redness, or necrosis. There are no lesions on the face, scalp, or tip of the nose, and the eyes are clear. Neurologic exam is non-focal and strength is normal.

Labs from today show creatinine 1.5 with an eGFR of 43, hemoglobin 13.8, and WBC 7.2.

Impression: Herpes zoster of the right T8 dermatome, uncomplicated, within 72 hours of rash onset, in an 82-year-old with CKD stage 3 and mildly elevated blood pressure from pain.

Management: Start valacyclovir for 7 days. The usual dose is 1000 mg three times daily, but because his eGFR is 43 I reduced it to 1000 mg every 12 hours. Continue acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed. Start gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime for nerve pain, with titration at follow-up and dosing adjusted for his kidney function. Add lidocaine 5% patches to the painful skin for 12 hours on and 12 hours off. Avoid NSAIDs because of his CKD. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and recheck blood pressure at follow-up. Keep the rash clean, dry, and covered, and avoid contact with infants and with anyone who is immunocompromised or has never had chickenpox until the lesions crust. I will give the recombinant zoster vaccine after he recovers, in about two to three months. He should call right away for eye pain, new facial rash, fever, or spreading redness, and we will see him back in one week to assess pain and the risk of postherpetic neuralgia.

The patient is a 42-year-old male seen in the outpatient psychiatry clinic for follow-up of panic disorder, which has worsened over the past month. He returned about ten days ago from a three-week trip overseas to visit relatives that included two long-haul flights. He ran out of his sertraline early in the trip and was unable to refill it afterward because the copay was more than he could afford. Since then he has had recurrent panic attacks, about four per week, including one on the flight home, with sudden pounding heart, sweating, shortness of breath, trembling, chest tightness, and fear of dying that peak within ten minutes. He also reports dizziness, nausea, and brief electric-shock sensations in the head that began a few days after the sertraline ran out, which fits SSRI discontinuation symptoms. He initially told me he had been taking sertraline 100 mg daily, but later in the visit he clarified that for the last two months he had been splitting the 100 mg tablets and taking only 50 mg daily to stretch the supply.

While overseas he bought alprazolam 0.5 mg tablets from a pharmacy without a prescription and has been taking one up to twice daily for the past week, with only brief relief. He also takes pseudoephedrine 60 mg every 6 hours as needed for nasal congestion since the flight. He completed a course of atovaquone-proguanil, one tablet daily, for malaria prophylaxis, finishing seven days after his return. He denies fever, diarrhea, and cough since returning.

Other history includes HTN treated with lisinopril 20 mg daily, hyperlipidemia, and GERD treated with omeprazole 20 mg daily. He has not taken his atorvastatin 20 mg daily for about two months because of cost. He drinks about two beers per week, drinks three cups of coffee a day, and uses no recreational drugs. He denies suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, hallucinations, and decreased need for sleep.

Last week his primary care physician obtained an ECG showing normal sinus rhythm with normal intervals, TSH 1.9, hemoglobin 14.6, and glucose 94. Today his BP is 136/88, HR 88, RR 16, and SpO2 99% on room air. On mental status exam he is anxious but cooperative, with normal speech, an anxious affect, linear thought process, no psychotic symptoms, and good insight. PHQ-9 is 6 and GAD-7 is 15.

My impression is panic disorder with recurrent panic attacks that worsened after he interrupted sertraline, with SSRI discontinuation symptoms, and contribution from unprescribed alprazolam use, pseudoephedrine, and caffeine. He also has HTN, hyperlipidemia, and GERD, and the missed doses of medication were driven by cost.

Management: Restart sertraline at 50 mg daily, with a plan to increase to 100 mg daily after one week if he tolerates it; the clinic pharmacist will use a low-cost generic program so the monthly cost is minimal. Discontinue alprazolam, because it is not prescribed and risks dependence; he will discard the remaining tablets. Stop pseudoephedrine and limit caffeine to one cup daily. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily, and ask his primary care physician to address the generic atorvastatin. Refer to the clinic social worker for help with medication costs. Start weekly cognitive behavioral therapy for panic disorder, with breathing retraining and interoceptive exposure. Because he recently traveled, I advised him that any fever in the next three months needs prompt medical evaluation. Return in two weeks, sooner for worsening symptoms or any thoughts of self-harm.

note:
Chief Complaint: Sudden severe headache.

HPI: 40-year-old female with hypertension, migraine, and current tobacco use who presents with a sudden severe headache that began about two hours ago while she was carrying groceries up a flight of stairs. She describes it as the worst headache of her life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds, located at the back of her head and radiating into the neck. She has had nausea with one episode of vomiting and mild neck stiffness. She first told the triage nurse she took sumatriptan 100 mg at home with no relief; on further questioning she clarified that she took one 50 mg tablet, not 100 mg. She says this is different from her usual migraines, which are one-sided and throbbing. She denies head trauma, fever, vision loss, double vision, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, seizure, and loss of consciousness.

She lives alone, has no family nearby, and has few people she can call. She has not taken amlodipine 10 mg daily or lisinopril 20 mg daily for about one month because she could not afford the refills. She smokes about ten cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol rarely.

ROS: Positive for nausea. Negative for chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, dysuria, and rash.

Physical Exam: Vitals BP 188/104, HR 96, RR 18, temp 98.6 F, SpO2 98% on room air. Uncomfortable, lying still in a dark room. Mild neck stiffness with flexion, no Kernig or Brudzinski sign. Pupils equal and reactive, fundi without papilledema, cranial nerves II through XII intact, strength 5/5 in all extremities, sensation intact, finger-to-nose normal, gait steady. Heart regular without murmur. Lungs clear.

ED Course / Results: CT head without contrast about three hours after onset showed no hemorrhage, mass, or hydrocephalus. CT angiography of the head and neck showed no aneurysm, dissection, or vessel narrowing. Labs: WBC 8.9, hemoglobin 13.4, platelets 262, sodium 139, potassium 3.9, creatinine 0.8, glucose 102, INR 1.0, troponin negative, urine pregnancy test negative. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy. She received acetaminophen 1000 mg by mouth, metoclopramide 10 mg IV, and labetalol 10 mg IV once; BP improved to 164/92 and her headache improved from 9 out of 10 to 4 out of 10.

Medical Decision Making: Thunderclap headache, with subarachnoid hemorrhage the leading concern. A non-contrast CT within six hours of onset and a normal CT angiogram effectively exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage, and I discussed the option of lumbar puncture with the patient, who preferred not to have one. I also considered cervical artery dissection and aneurysm (negative on CTA), meningitis (afebrile, low suspicion), venous sinus thrombosis, and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, which can follow triptan use; for this reason sumatriptan is discontinued until she is evaluated by neurology. Hypertensive emergency is unlikely with no papilledema, normal creatinine, and negative troponin, but her BP is elevated because she has been off her antihypertensives. Final impression is thunderclap headache with negative CT and CTA, likely a migraine variant aggravated by uncontrolled hypertension, with medication non-adherence due to cost.

Disposition: Because she lives alone, I offered observation; she stayed in the ED observation unit for six more hours with repeat neurologic checks, her headache settled to 2 out of 10, and BP was 148/88 at discharge. Restart lisinopril 20 mg daily, and restart amlodipine at a reduced dose of 5 mg daily rather than 10 mg since she has been off it for a month. Sumatriptan is discontinued. Social work arranged enrollment in a medication assistance program, a $4 generic list for her refills, a sliding-scale community clinic, and a taxi voucher home. A nurse will phone her within 24 hours since no one will be with her tonight. Follow up with primary care in 3 days for a BP check and neurology within 2 weeks. Strict return precautions given: call 911 for a new severe headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, weakness, trouble speaking, or seizure. Counseled to stop smoking.

He reports about six weeks of chest pressure when he climbs two flights of stairs or walks briskly uphill. It lasts roughly three minutes and goes away with rest. The pattern has been the same each time and has not worsened. He denies chest pain at rest, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea, and leg swelling. He also denies lightheadedness during the episodes.

He drinks heavily, about eight beers a day for several years, with the last drink yesterday evening. He denies tremor, sweating, or other withdrawal symptoms today. He does not smoke and uses no recreational drugs.

Past history is significant for hypertension that has not been treated and hyperlipidemia. His father had a heart attack at 52, correction, at 54. He takes aspirin 81 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and that is all.

On exam, blood pressure 148/92, heart rate 84, weight 232 pounds, BMI 32. Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, no gallop, lungs clear, no jugular venous distension, no peripheral edema, and the liver edge is palpable and mildly tender. Resting ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with no ST changes and no Q waves. Labs from last week: LDL 142 on atorvastatin 40 mg, AST 62 and ALT 48, hemoglobin A1c 5.7, creatinine 0.9.

Impression, one, stable exertional angina, probable obstructive coronary artery disease given the typical symptoms and his risk factors. Two, heavy alcohol use, with probable alcohol-related liver injury given the elevated AST and ALT. Three, hypertension, untreated, and hyperlipidemia not at goal.

Management. Start metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily for angina and blood pressure. Increase atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg daily. Continue aspirin 81 mg daily. Prescribe nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual as needed for chest pain; I reviewed how to take it and to call 911 if the pain does not resolve five minutes after one dose. Start thiamine 100 mg daily. Order a treadmill nuclear stress test and a transthoracic echocardiogram. If the stress test is abnormal we will proceed to coronary angiography. I counseled him at length on cutting back on alcohol and offered a referral to an addiction medicine clinic and counseling, which he accepted; he should not stop drinking abruptly without medical advice given his daily intake. Avoid heavy exertion until testing is complete. Return to clinic in two weeks after the stress test, and sooner for any rest pain, syncope, or worsening symptoms.
summary: A 43-year-old male who drinks about eight beers a day has had six weeks of exertional chest pressure lasting about three minutes and relieved by rest, with no rest pain, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea or leg swelling. He has untreated hypertension and hyperlipidemia, with BP 148/92, a normal resting ECG, LDL 142, and AST 62 and ALT 48. The impression is stable exertional angina with probable coronary disease, heavy alcohol use and uncontrolled risk factors. Metoprolol succinate, sublingual nitroglycerin and thiamine are started, atorvastatin is increased to 80 mg, aspirin continues, a treadmill nuclear stress test and echocardiogram are ordered, and addiction medicine referral and a two-week return are arranged.

Hospital day 2 for a 56-year-old male admitted after a syncopal episode. Yesterday morning he stood up quickly from the toilet after several days of poor oral intake and loose stools from a presumed viral gastroenteritis. He had a few seconds of lightheadedness and tunnel vision, then lost consciousness for roughly thirty seconds, witnessed by his wife, who denies any shaking, incontinence, or tongue biting. He recovered quickly without confusion and has a small scalp abrasion but no head injury of concern. He denies chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, focal weakness, and melena. He has a 35-pack-year history and currently smokes one pack per day.

Overnight there were no events. Telemetry has shown sinus rhythm at 60 to 90 beats per minute with no pauses, no atrial or ventricular arrhythmia, and no nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. He is receiving 0.9% saline at 100 mL per hour after a 1 liter bolus on admission, and a nicotine patch 21 mg/24 hours was started yesterday. At home he takes amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily; lisinopril was held on admission.

Vitals today are temperature 98.2 F, heart rate 70, respiratory rate 16, and SpO2 97% on room air. Orthostatics on admission were supine BP 128/78 with heart rate 70, and standing at three minutes BP 98/62 with heart rate 96, with lightheadedness. Today's standing BP is 112/70 with heart rate 82 and no symptoms. His mucous membranes were dry yesterday and are moist today. Heart has a regular rhythm without murmurs, carotid arteries have no bruits, lungs are clear, and the neurologic exam is non-focal.

Data: troponin was negative twice. ECG shows sinus rhythm at 68 with normal intervals and no ST changes. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 60% with no significant valve disease or wall motion abnormality. Hemoglobin 14.2, sodium 138, potassium 4.0, glucose 104. Creatinine was 1.4 on admission and is 1.1 today, with BUN 30 on admission.

Impression: Syncope most consistent with orthostatic hypotension due to volume depletion on top of antihypertensive therapy. Cardiac syncope is less likely given the reassuring ECG, telemetry, echocardiogram, and troponins. He also has a prerenal acute kidney injury that is improving, HTN, and tobacco use.

Management: Stop IV fluids this evening if he continues to take adequate oral fluids. Continue to hold lisinopril. Reduce amlodipine from 10 mg to 5 mg daily. Continue nicotine patch 21 mg/24 hours, and I counseled him on smoking cessation and offered a quitline referral. Continue atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Physical therapy evaluation and ambulation with fall precautions; he was instructed to rise slowly. Repeat BMP in the morning. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if standing BP stays stable, with a primary care visit in one week to recheck BMP and a home BP log, and a decision on restarting lisinopril.
